newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices take a dive as Iraq steps back.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices take a dive as Iraq steps back.

text.p: World oil prices rose sharply on Friday amid expectations of an imminent U.S. attack against Iraqi targets but the rally came to an abrupt halt after Baghdad appeared to step back from a confrontation with Washington.

October futures for world benchmark Brent Blend crude clung to near five-year highs throughout much of the day as nervous oil traders showed little inclination to sell amid widespread anticipation of a U.S. strike against Iraq at the weekend.

But with the October contract expiring on Friday night, November took the brunt of a sell-off as dealers liquidated long positions after Iraq suspended threats to shoot at Western planes patrolling Iraq.

The Iraqi ruling Revolutionary Command Council issued a statement shortly after U.S. Stealth bombers landed in neighbouring Kuwait saying Iraq would suspend attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes flying over northern and southern no-fly zones as of midnight local time (2000 GMT).
The U.S. Pentagon described the move as encouraging but said it would watch the situation carefully.
November Brent was at 1815 GMT trading down 74 cents at $22.72 a barrel. It dumped 41 cents immediately after the news came out of Baghdad. October Brent fell back to $24.05 barrels, up 18 cents.
"This is a political market now and it's a little bit like a casino. It is very emotional," said Charles Grey of Prudential Bache.

Earlier on Friday, October Brent traded as high as $24.27 a barrel, up 40 cents on the day and only 15 cents off Wednesday's peak. This was the highest prompt price on London's International Petroleum Exchange since January 1991 when U.S.-led allies launched their successful Gulf war to end Iraqi occupation of Kuwait.

Oil prices rallied nearly $2 a barrel this week as military action over Iraq raised fears of disruption to vital fuel supplies from the Gulf, which contains nearly 70 percent of the world's oil reserves and accounts for about a quarter of output.

"The problem is that Saudi Arabia is about the only oil producer who has spare capacity so any tension in that area is likely to keep prices firm," said Bob Finch, head of trading in London at oil-trading and refining company Vitol SA.
Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil producer and exporter and its 8.0 million barrel per day (bpd) output makes use of about 80 percent of its capacity.
Extension of the conflict to neighbouring producer Kuwait -- which anaylsts consider unlikely given the might of the U.S. military presence in the region -- would drive prices considerably higher.

But even without a significant escalation of the conflict, traders and analysts do not expect prices to retreat in the short term as western demand gathers pace ahead of winter, industry stocks stay low and non-OPEC supply disappoints.

The indefinite postponement of a U.N. deal that would allow Baghdad's return to the oil market in a limited capacity for the first time since its invasion of Kuwait nearly six years ago would also continue to provide solid support, they said.

The accord, signed on May 20, would have allowed Iraq to sell some $2 billion worth of oil over six months -- equivalent to about 700,000 bpd -- to raise money for food and other much-needed humanitarian supplies.

"Given the approaching U.S. presidential elections, it now seems increasingly likely that Iraqi oil exports will remain shut off until at least early 1997, which in turn adds up to a "loss' of 60-80 million barrels of Iraqi oil," said Kleinwort Benson in a market report.
